title: Chapter 21 – The Refiner's Bench
html:
"It will not take," says Third Aunt.

She says it kindly, with her hands in a basin of herb water and her sleeves pinned back, and she does not look up from the green leaves she is washing. Lin Wenqing's workroom is the warmest in the Hollow, a long low room off the herb garden where drying bundles hang from every rafter and her Yellow Grade cauldron squats on its iron tripod like a patient toad. A Heat Plate glows on the floor under it, the same cheap talisman a baker's boy uses at Willow Ford, steady and even, because Third Aunt believes in flame that does not need watching.

Lin Jian sits on a stool by the shelf, with a slate in his lap and a stub of chalk. He has been drawing for an hour.

"Father's channels are torn, Third Aunt. Not bruised. Four of them, on the left side, ten years ago."

"I know what they are, child. I set the splints." She lifts a leaf and turns it to the light. "A Green Pulse Pill is a Level One, high grade. It does one thing: it helps damaged channels that are still viable knit themselves together. A viable channel has two ends close enough to find each other." She sets the leaf down. "Your father's ends are a hand's breadth apart. The scar between them is as dead as a rope. I have brewed Green Pulse for him three times in ten years, and three times he has swallowed it, and three times it has run through him like water through a sieve."

"What if there were something for the gap?"

She does look up then, finally, and her dark eyes rest on his slate.

On it, in chalk, is a pill. Not the shape of one, but the logic: a column of herbs down the left, a column of effects down the right, and a line from each to each. The standard recipe sits at the top, phoenix ash and red lotus and a heat-resistant crystal, the oldest Green Pulse formula in the compendium. Below it, circled twice, is a short list of things that grow on the slopes above the Hollow and have never been put in a pill.

Jade-vein fern. Frostbell moss. Blood-stop grass. A trace of cinnabar-iron.

"Where did you get this?" she says.

"I read your herb ledgers while I was doing the sums for Wenhai." This is true. "Everything you wrote about the north gully. The ferns that glow in the shade."

"I wrote that they were useless."

"You wrote that they conduct. That if you lay a frond across a Spirit Lantern chip, the light runs along the vein and not across the leaf. You thought it was pretty." He turns the slate toward her. "A meridian is a vein. A torn one is a vein with a gap. If a frond could carry Qi across a gap in a Lantern, maybe it could carry it across a gap in a man."

Third Aunt says nothing for a long, long time. Then she dries her hands on her apron, slowly, finger by finger, and crosses the room to look at the slate from two paces.

"Where does the stone go?" she says.

"One mid-grade spirit stone per pill. It is the spark. The fern carries the Qi; the stone makes it run." He hesitates. "I think three pills would give Father back about half of what he lost."

"Half."

"Not all. I do not know a recipe for all."

"Half," says Third Aunt, and a thing comes into her face that Lin Jian has not seen there since the day Bo's pyre was lit. She puts a hand over her mouth. When she takes it away, her voice is perfectly even. "Three mid-grade stones. The treasury has none. I will make the pills if you bring me the herbs. And the stones."

"Yes, Third Aunt."

"And Jian." She taps the slate with one finger. "You will not tell your father until I have the first pill in my hand. If it fails, he has had ten years of hope broken once already. I will not break him a fourth time."

* * *

The north gully lies two hours above the frostbell slopes, in a fold of shadow where the sun reaches for perhaps one hour in the day. It is deep, mossy, wet with seeps, and as silent as a tomb. Lin Jian stands at its lip with a bone knife in his hand, and Kai beside him with a lantern, and thinks that in all the places the Hollow has hidden things, this one might be the best.

The ferns are there.

They fill the gully floor in a pale green sea, fronds as long as his forearm and as translucent as jade, and down the center of each, a dark, glowing vein. In the gloom, it looks as if a thousand small green rivers have been poured into the earth and left to shine.

Scan.

```
[Scan — Jade-Vein Fern]
Tissue: translucent, silica-reinforced fronds
Central vein: Qi conductivity 0.72 (human meridian tissue: 0.68–0.80)
Structural match: meridian bridging, 61%
Toxicity: none
Note: cut with bone/horn only (metal blades short the vein)
CE: +4
```

Sixty-one percent. It is not perfect. But it is the best match he has ever seen for a thing the world has not named, and for the first time since the morning Father said a hand's breadth, no more, Lin Jian lets himself believe it.

"What does it say?" Kai asks, shifting the lantern.

"That it is pretty." He kneels. "Hold the light still."

They cut for an hour. The knife, bone, as the scan says, slides through the frond like a thumb through butter, and each stem comes away with a faint chime, like a struck glass. They fill two bags, and Kai grumbles, and they climb out of the gully into a gray rain that has begun to fall without either of them noticing.

* * *

Old Hu melts the blade on the day before Lin Jian's birthday.

He does it alone at first, in the forge, with the door barred and the bellows going and the heat in the room a thick hard thing that presses on the ears. Lin Jian is not supposed to be there. He is there because Hu, at the last moment, put his head out and said, without looking at him, "You may sit by the wall and keep your mouth shut."

So he sits, with his knees drawn up, as the old man lays the curved blade on a bed of coals.

It takes four hours. Lin Jian has watched Hu forge a hundred things, plowshares and hinges and the iron rim of a well, but he has never seen him work like this. The old man does not hurry. He does not speak. He moves around the coals as a doctor moves around a sickbed, turning, listening, adding charcoal in measured scoops, and the blade lies in the red heart of the fire and does not melt.

It resists.

That is the only word. The steel reddens, and then whitens, and then should slump into a river of light, and instead it holds its shape, rigid and bright, like a thing that has decided not to die. The air above it shimmers. A thin wail, high and inhuman, begins to rise from the coals.

"That is the quench," Hu says. His voice is steady, but there is sweat in the lines of his face. "The elder's blood. It is in the grain of the iron. It does not want to be iron. It wants to be what it was."

Lin Jian looks at the blade with his Spirit Sense, and he sees it. A web of fine red threads runs through the bright steel, pulling tight against the heat. A lattice. The same pattern that sits, cold and dormant, in the skin of his left ankle.

Scan.

```
[Scan — Sha, Melt State]
Material: spirit iron (Profound grade core), bone-carbon alloy
Contaminant: blood-lattice, Blood Shadow type, 11.4% of mass
Lattice behavior: resists thermal change; reinforces crystal structure
Hu's furnace: 1,640 C (insufficient to dissolve lattice)
Recommended: SEPARATE lattice from iron (non-living material, Level 2 OK)
Cost: 10 CE (remaining: 108 / 400)
```

Eleven percent. A web of dead blood as fine as spider silk, holding the steel together against the fire. If it could be lifted out, the iron beneath would be clean, plain, and willing. And Hu has been standing at this fire for three hours, sweating, trying to boil it away.

I could end this in a breath.

He looks at the old man's face, at the gray at the temples, the missing arm, the one stubborn eye. And he thinks of the thing Hu told Mother in the sickroom: I have never in my life melted down a thing I made well. Hu does not want to be rescued from this. He wants to finish it. But he is an old man, and the forge is hot, and there is a boy sitting against the wall with a power in his head that nobody in the world has a name for.

"Master Hu."

"Quiet."

"The threads are pulling against the cold side of the blade, not the hot. If you flip it, and put the edge on the coals instead of the spine, and then quench the spine in water, the lattice will tear along the fold. The grain runs the wrong way for it."

Hu does not move. The sweat runs into his eye. He does not wipe it.

"Say that again," he says.

Lin Jian says it again.

The old man grunts, once. Then he gets the tongs under the blade and flips it, edge-down in the coals, and the wail rises to a scream, and he plunges the spine into the trough beside him, and the whole room fills with white steam.

When it clears, the blade has split.

It has not broken. It has opened along the fold, like a pod, and out of the crack runs a thin glittering thread of red that coils on the coals, hisses, and goes black. And Lin Jian, with one hand flat on his knee and his eyes half closed, pulls on the other thread, the one only he can see, and thinks, very quietly:

Separate.

The red lattice lifts out of the iron like smoke out of a chimney and dissolves in the air. The scream stops.

Silence in the forge. The bellows wheeze. A last bead of metal sags from the open blade and drips on the coals.

"It's just iron," Hu says. His voice has gone odd. "It's just iron again."

He sets the tongs down. He puts his one hand flat on the anvil and leans on it, and for a long moment, he does not look like a legend or a refiner or a man with a dozen secrets. He looks like what he is, which is an old man who has been carrying a weight for twenty years and has just felt it lift.

"You did that," he says, not turning.

"I told you where the grain ran."

"Hm." A pause. "Ask me how I know that is not the whole truth."

"How do you know?"

"I don't." The old eye turns, finally, and rests on the boy. "I have decided not to."

* * *

The ingot comes out of the mold the next dawn, a black-gray bar the length of a forearm, plain and heavy and faintly warm. Hu does not name it. He wraps it in a scrap of oilcloth and walks it across the compound himself, one-armed, with his rod under his arm, and sets it on the council table in front of Grandfather.

"Sell it," he says. "Buy a pill."

Grandfather looks at the bar. He does not touch it.

"It was your finest work," he says.

"It was my worst. I did not know that until I'd made it." Hu's mouth moves in something that is not a smile. "It is iron now. It does not remember what it was. Take it to Mo, and tell him to give you a fair price, and if he does not, tell him I will make him a fair price."

For the first time in Lin Jian's memory, the Patriarch of the Lin clan stands up from his chair and bows to a man who is not of his blood.

"Thank you," he says.

It is two words. It is, Lin Jian understands, the whole of what the old man has been trying to say since the day they met.

"Just don't die in the attempt," Hu says gruffly, and goes out.

Deacon Mo comes up from Willow Ford three days later, hat in hand, round and nervous and sweating, to inspect the bar. He turns it over, runs a thumb along its grain, and lets out a long low whistle. He pays two hundred and twenty low-grade stones, in a hemp bag that clinks like a tinker's cart, and does not haggle once.

The treasury, with the cave box and the ingot, now stands past the price of a Sect-furnace Foundation Establishment pill, which is four hundred. The market pills sold in Willow Ford at a hundred and twenty are another thing, Grandfather says: cheap, unstable, brewed in a back alley. Seven in ten fail, and the three that do not leave the drinker with a foundation like a cracked bowl. He will not stake his life on a pill that has a three in ten chance of being soup.

The order goes to the Azure Cloud Sect's Alchemy Pavilion that afternoon. The pill will be delivered, sealed, at the beginning of summer.

"And the attempt?" Third Aunt asks at the council.

"At midsummer," says Grandfather. "On the longest day, in the chamber below the hall." He glances, for just an instant, down the table. "And I will not be announcing the date to anyone who does not already know it."

Second Uncle, three seats down, writes nothing in his notebook. His pen does not move.

* * *

Lin Jian's ninth birthday begins before dawn, with a spear.

Lin Feng is waiting for him on the threshing floor in the gray cold, with a long stave of ash wood in each hand. It is a plain thing, seven feet of straight-grained wood with a blunt iron cap, scarred by use. Feng holds one out, haft-first.

"Happy birthday, little cousin."

Lin Jian takes it. It is lighter than it looks, perfectly balanced, and the wood under his palm has a smoothness that comes only from hands. "This is yours."

"It was mine. Mine now is steel." Feng's mouth twitches. "Ash is for learning. You do not break your grip on steel the first week." He steps back and sets his feet. "I have been watching you fight with your hands and your pins and your tricks, and you fight like a clever merchant. I want to teach you to fight like a Lin. Do you want to learn?"

"Yes."

"Then guard."

It is the first of what will be many dawns. Feng is fifteen and a Qi Refining Seventh Stage cultivator, with a ring of fire at his shoulder and a spear that moves like a snake, and for an hour he beats Lin Jian across the frozen floor with the flat of an ash stave until his arms are numb and his ribs are blue. He does not say a kind word. At the end he stands over his cousin, breathing hard, and says, "Better."

"I fell down four times."

"You got up five."

It is the nicest thing Feng has ever said to him.

* * *

The gifts are laid out at breakfast, on the long table, with the whole family looking on.

Lin Yue's is first. She has made it herself, with a great deal of help from Old Nan, and she presents it with a tremendous gravity: a crown of dried jade-vein fern, woven into a ring, with the central veins arranged to catch the light. It is slightly lopsided. It glows faintly, in the shade of his hands, like a thousand tiny green rivers.

"Because you like them," she says. "You cut them."

"I do like them."

"You are supposed to wear it."

He wears it. The whole table laughs.

Father's is a new inkstone, a smooth black slab of Willow Ford slate with a pine-leaf carving along the rim, and a small bronze weight for pressing paper. "The old one is mine," he says, with a sidelong glance. "This is for yours. I think you will want to draw your own talismans soon."

Mother's is a pair of boots. Plain, high, cut from supple dark leather and stitched twice at the seam, reaching to the middle of the calf. She sets them on the table without comment. Lin Jian turns them over, and sees at once that the lining is smooth, that the tops are tall enough to cover the ankle bone, and that someone has sewn a hidden pocket in the left one, big enough for a folded paper.

He looks up. Her face tells him nothing at all.

"They will keep your feet dry," she says.

"Thank you, Mother."

Hu's is last. He does not bring it to the table. He sits at the end of the bench, with his rod across his knees and his porridge going cold, and when the family has finished and the laughter has died, he reaches into his belt with his one hand and sets it on the boards between the bowls.

A knife, palm-long, in a sheath of black leather. The handle is horn, bound in fine copper wire. The blade, when Lin Jian draws it, is a plain dark gray, and it shines with the subtle, restless glow of true spirit iron. Yellow Grade. A real weapon, in the hands of a nine-year-old. He stares at it.

"The bar was too much to waste," Hu says. "I cut a finger's length from the end before I gave it to Mo. This is what I made of that." He looks away. "Yours was made from my worst one. I think it will be my best."

Nobody at the table says anything. Mother's eyes move to the knife and back to Hu's face, and something passes between them that Lin Jian cannot read.

"Don't cut your thumb off," Hu says. "I have only the one left."

* * *

On the night of his ninth birthday, Lin Jian stands in the middle of the quarry over the carcass of a tusk boar.

He has gone there alone, as he goes alone most evenings now, with a leather sack of pins and the new knife at his belt and the ash spear in his hand. There is a pen at the head of the quarry, built last winter by Feng and Dong from fence rails, in which they have kept a dozen low-tier beasts for the junior cousins to test their talismans on. Tonight it holds a two-hundred-pound tusk boar, mud-gray and bristled, with a pair of yellowed tusks as long as Lin Jian's forearm. It is the kind of animal a farmer fears and a cultivator treats as an exercise.

He does not treat it as an exercise.

He treats it as Hu has taught him: as a problem, with a cause. The boar charges in a straight line, always, because its neck is too thick to turn quickly. It drops its head at ten paces. It favors the left tusk. Lin Jian has been watching the same animal for six nights, from the other side of the rails, and counting.

So he puts a seventy-eight percent pin in the dirt at eight paces, because the pin does not need to hold, only to catch. He steps back. He raises the ash spear. And when the boar's head dips, he does three things at once. He fires a thread of water from the shaping seal of the Tidal Spear, as thin as a needle, into the soft pad behind its left tusk. He drops into Cloudstep and slides sideways across the packed dirt. And he plants the butt of the spear against the quarry wall and lets the boar run onto the iron cap.

It is clumsy. It is not elegant. The cap catches the animal in the shoulder instead of the throat, and the force goes up his arms and nearly takes the spear out of his hands. But it goes down, and it does not get up, and Lin Jian stands over it with his heart going like a drum and his hands shaking.

Two hundred pounds of pork, he thinks. And I did not even use the knife.

```
[Scan — Tusk Boar (first rank, medium tier)]
Weak point: left tusk root, nerve cluster (confirmed)
Tissue: dense, low Qi
CE: +3 (total: 111 / 400)
```

Then something in his body gives a long, soft click, like a key turning.

It begins in his belly. A warmth, a spreading, a feeling of being filled to the top of a vessel whose rim he did not know was there. His Qi, which has been gathering in him for months, a slow cold accumulation like water behind a dam, suddenly finds the dam is gone. It runs through him from crown to heel. It lights his eyes. And the world, which a moment before was gray and close, opens like a window.

Sixth stage.

It is slower than the last one. Jian knows that; he has watched the numbers all winter. The fifth stage came in a week of nights after the Walking Elm, because the Qi was waiting for him. The sixth has taken three months of grinding, and the seventh, he understands, will take more. The jump from five to six is a step. From six to seven will be a climb.

He lets out a long breath, and the pale cloud of it drifts over the dead boar and the dark stone and the stars. Forty paces is no longer the limit of what he can feel. He can feel the whole quarry. He can feel the wall, and the terraces below it, and the soft sleeping lights of the hill, and beyond them, faint and far, the line of the stream.

And at the foot of the hill, where the old brick kiln stands, a single hooded lantern.

* * *

He knows it before he sees it.

Spirit Sense does not show him a picture. It gives him a presence, a warmth in the cold, a shape of Qi moving down the far slope. It is a man. It is walking. It is walking carefully, with a parcel on its back, the way a man walks when he does not want to be heard.

Wenhai.

He does not need the lantern to know. He has been tracking the shape of that Qi for months, ever since the evening in the library. It is tight, smooth, tidy, a fist in a glove, and it is the only thing in the valley that moves like a ledger.

He slips down the quarry wall and through the terraces in Cloudstep, with the new boots soundless on the frozen mud. He stops forty paces from the kiln and lies flat behind a retaining wall.

The kiln is the oldest ruin on the hill, a squat brick dome on the lowest terrace, unused for twenty years. The roof has fallen in. Weeds grow from the firing mouth. Wenhai kneels at its north side, with his lantern shuttered to a slit, and works four loose bricks out of the wall with a small iron bar. He slides a heavy oilcloth bag into the space behind them. He replaces the bricks. He sits back on his heels and presses his palm flat against the wall, as if in prayer.

Then he takes a long, long time to stand.

Lin Jian watches him go. He waits a hundred breaths. He crosses the terrace on his belly, as Hu taught him, and lays his palm on the same bricks.

Scan.

```
[Scan — Brick Cavity, North Wall]
Contents: oilcloth bag (canvas, double-waxed)
- 211 low-grade spirit stones
- 3 mid-grade spirit stones
- 1 letter, Zhao family of Red Ridge seal (red wax, jagged ridge under rising sun)
- 1 ledger, 40 entries, hand: Lin Wenhai
Matches: Wenhai's skimming ledger, 91%
CE: +3 (total: 114 / 400)
```

Three mid-grade stones.

He stares at the figure for a long moment, and the cold, quiet part of his mind, the part that has never once told him a comfortable thing, adds it up without being asked. Three stones for three pills. Father's channels, half returned. And they are sitting in a hole in a wall, behind four loose bricks, in the bag of the man who sold the family's deed to Zhao.

Evidence, a letter, and the cure.

He does not touch the bricks. He wipes the mud from his sleeve, and stands. The kiln is silent. A bat flits through the broken roof. His breath makes a small cloud in the dark.

He turns, and there is a figure in the shadow of the terrace wall, ten paces behind him.

Spirit Sense finds nothing. She is wearing the gray short robe, her hood is up, and her Qi is folded so small that it might be a stone's. But he hears her, the faintest slow breath, and he feels her. It is the stillness of a person who has been watching for some time, and a flat calm behind it that he knows better than his own name.

"Jian," says his mother, very quietly.

"Mother."

She steps out of the dark, and the starlight finds her face. She is not angry. She is not afraid. She looks, if anything, curious, in the grave unhurried way she has when she is counting something.

"It is after midnight," she says. "You are nine years old. And you have just walked to a ruined kiln in the dark, without a lamp, and put your hand on a particular brick."

He says nothing.

"How do you know what is inside, Jian?" she says. "In the dark. Without a light."

The wind moves over the terraces. Somewhere far off, a dog barks twice and falls silent.

Lin Jian opens his mouth, and finds that he has no answer at all.
